articles.title: What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.00018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Role-specialized QA pipelines increasingly pass rationales from a reasoner to a verifier, but it is unclear what this message actually buys: better answers, stronger support assessment, or a new failure surface. We introduce a message-intervention diagnostic that fixes the evidence and candidate answer while varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. articles.title: Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.00002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce reverse Item Response Theory (IRT) to pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by treating cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC2) database, the model estimates cancer-type-level in-vitro resistance and drug-level broad activity on a shared latent scale. Validation across four missingness regimes demonstrates that reverse IRT better recovers the full-data latent ranking

articles.title: How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.00004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adam is the standard optimizer in deep learning, yet its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) contains unresolved questions. We study Adam's full update rule, including momentum, as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant $\gamma(\Delta\theta)$ metric, we measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression

articles.title: Curious people tend to have more of the experiences linked to cognitive reserve, study finds
articles.summary: A new study suggests that curious people build more "cognitive reserve" through higher education and mentally stimulating hobbies. However, this curiosity didn't translate into higher scores on cognitive tests among the healthy adults studied.

articles.title: Scientists reveal the brain’s hidden role in building exercise endurance
articles.summary: Building physical stamina isn't just about training your muscles. A new study reveals that specific cells in the brain coordinate the body's metabolic adaptations to exercise, playing a central role in boosting athletic endurance over time.

articles.title: What It’s Like to Be…a Hotshot
articles.summary: Digging line to redirect the country's fiercest wildland fires, sleeping in the dirt after a 16-hour day, and turning physical endurance into a public service with Ben Strahan, a hotshot crew superintendent in California. What does a wildfire sound like up close? And where does a crew go when the fire threatens to overrun them? articles.title: Longitudinal study highlights the enduring toll of childhood loneliness and social isolation
articles.summary: New research challenges the idea that loneliness acts as a helpful alarm bell. A 6-year study found that feeling lonely does not motivate isolated children to reconnect, and both issues independently harm future mental health and career prospects.

articles.title: Financial and relationship worries predict bad dreams
articles.summary: People experiencing high levels of daily stress are more likely to have negative emotions during their dreams. A recent study found that daytime coping mechanisms do not seem to alter this nighttime emotional carryover.

articles.title: The right side of the brain shows more signs of aging than the left, new study suggests
articles.summary: A new AI tool that analyzes MRI scans in fine detail reveals that the human brain does not age evenly. Some regions appear to age faster than others, with these differences becoming more pronounced in people with Alzheimer’s disease.

articles.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
articles.summary: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

articles.title: Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
articles.summary: A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause.

articles.title: Gut bacteria and digestive metabolites are linked to psychopathic traits
articles.summary: Specific bacteria in the human gut and mouth, along with digestive byproducts, are associated with psychopathic personality traits. The findings suggest the microbiome might influence how humans process emotions and regulate impulsive behavior.
